1:
Who the men from Judea were they answer only so far. Gill says they were not sent by the apostles but came of themselves, that who they were is not certain, that they were plainly judaizing teachers, and that according to Epiphanius they were Cerinthus and his followers. Barnes infers from their willingness to refer the dispute to the apostles that they had professedly embraced Christianity. Robertson identifies them with the party of the circumcision at Jerusalem, who volunteered without church action, their activity disclaimed by the conference itself, and recalls that Paul describes them with some heat as false brethren sneaked in to spy out our liberty. Ellicott adds that they came claiming to speak in the name of James, who distinctly repudiates having authorised them, and may have rested their case on his own rule that whoever keeps the whole law and offends in one point is guilty of all. Wesley supposes they came to supply what Paul and Barnabas had omitted; Clarke's block analyses the whole chapter.

Why the question revived after Cornelius they solve differently. Ellicott says those who objected to Peter's conduct were not content with the conclusion he drew, and to them the case may have seemed the exception that proved the rule: where signs and wonders came in they might accept an uncircumcised convert because God had dispensed with his own law; circumcision was an everlasting covenant never formally abrogated, and who were the new teachers to change what God had established? Robertson makes it scale rather than principle: they had acquiesced in the case of Cornelius after plain proof that it was the Lord's doing, but had not agreed to a campaign to turn the exception into the rule and make Christianity mainly Gentile with a few Jews instead of mainly Jewish with a few Gentiles.

Robertson alone relates this journey to the one Paul describes in Galatians, and names his opponent: it is reasonably certain that the visit of Galatians is this conference, against Ramsay's effort to identify it with the earlier famine visit, since Paul is not listing his visits but showing his independence of the twelve; Luke gives the outward narrative while Galatians shows the private interview, which fell between the public meeting and the deliberation.

What the episode signifies they treat as a lesson. Barnes calls it the first internal dissension in the church: hitherto they had struggled against external foes, but now the churches were at peace, and the great enemy of souls took occasion, as often since, to excite contentions within, so that what external violence could not destroy might be secured by internal strife; the history is further important as showing how such controversies were settled then. Henry says the same from the other side: even when things go smoothly it is folly to think the mountain stands strong, and if ever there was a heaven upon earth it was the church at Antioch then. Calvin presses it hardest: their doctrine was tried by domestic war as well as by professed enemies, and though we naturally abhor the cross, civil discord is the more dangerous, for when tyrants run violently the flesh is afraid but the conscience is not properly touched, whereas when the brethren go together by the ears weak minds must faint, especially when the controversy is about doctrine, the holy bond of brotherly unity; nothing does more damage to the gospel than civil discord, since it wounds weak consciences and gives the wicked occasion to backbite. Chrysostom sets the incident in a pattern: at every step of the Gentile mission the beginning is brought in as a matter of necessity, Peter having justified himself in the tone of apology, and Paul having turned to the Gentiles only when the Jews turned away, so that here too a law is enacted only because a new extravagance has come in.
2:
How sharp the quarrel was they measure by the word used. Barnes says the term rendered dissension can denote sedition or intestine war as well as earnest disputation, and holds that here it means warm discussion and no more. Robertson keeps the litotes, no little dissension and questioning; Calvin calls it no small trial that Paul and Barnabas should be haled into a troublesome tumult, there being mischief enough in the matter itself, and a crueller mischief when contention waxes so hot that men fight with brethren as with enemies. Clarke explains what they defended: Paul and Barnabas were satisfied that God did not design to bring the converted Gentiles under the yoke of circumcision, Christ being the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believed. Gill notes that as ministers of the uncircumcision they were witnesses of the grace bestowed and so advocates for the Gentiles.

Whether this is the journey of Galatians Wesley settles in a line: Paul's going up by revelation is very consistent with the account here, since the church in sending them might itself be so directed. Calvin observes that companions were joined to them by the common consent of the church, whence all the godly were plainly on their side and thought the cause their own. What being brought on their way meant Gill leaves open: either the brethren went part of the way with them out of respect, or the church provided things necessary. Clarke takes the second, since it does not appear they had property of their own; Barnes says it was customary for Christians to attend the apostles in their travels. Ellicott traces the route from Seleucia along the coast by Sidon and Tyre and probably Caesarea, then through Samaria, and notices what the choice implies, since they might have gone by Joppa and avoided both the old Canaanite cities and the hated Samaritans.

Who received them at Jerusalem they distinguish. Ellicott says the words imply a general gathering of the Church, members of different synagogues coming together with their presiding elders. Calvin makes the same division: by church is meant the multitude and the whole body, after which a peculiar place is assigned to the apostles and elders, by whom Paul and Barnabas were specially received. Robertson calls it a public reception at which the story could be heard; Barnes says they were acknowledged as Christian brethren and received with Christian kindness; Clarke identifies the apostles as the whole or part of the twelve, though we read of none but John, Peter and James; Wesley reduces it to two words: solemnly welcomed.

Whose speech the objection of the Pharisees is divides them. Barnes says it has been doubted whether these are the words of Paul and Barnabas relating what occurred at Antioch or Luke's own record of what took place at Jerusalem, and judges the correct exposition to refer them to Jerusalem. Clarke takes the other side outright: the verse appears to be part of the declaration made by Paul and Barnabas to the council, who having stated how God blessed their ministry proceed to declare how the good work was likely to be hindered. Calvin sides with the Jerusalem reading: Luke does not without cause say what kind of men went about to trouble Paul at Jerusalem, and the evil flowed from that fountain. Ellicott says this is the first distinct mention of any convert from the Pharisaic party, though the drift had begun during our Lord's ministry. Robertson says they rose out of the crowd at a critical moment, believers in Christ but still of the sect of the Pharisees; Gill notes only that this was the strictest sect among the Jews; Wesley draws the moral, that even believers are apt to retain their former turn of mind and its prejudices, and takes the law of Moses here for the whole law, moral and ritual.
6:
Who sat in the council runs four ways. Clarke says this was the first council ever held in the Christian Church, composed of the apostles and elders simply. Calvin agrees: Luke does not say the whole Church was gathered but those who excelled in doctrine and judgment and were by office lawful judges, though the disputation may have been held before the people. Barnes takes the other side, that the whole church was convened and at least concurred; Robertson infers the same from what follows; Gill says the private members were there, and that whether all the apostles attended is not certain, though Peter, James and John did. Ellicott goes furthest: presbyters had an equal voice with the apostles, whose position was that of the later bishops, and those whom we should call the laity were present and gave their vote, though there is no absolute proof they took part.

What kind of assembly it was Ellicott alone defines. It is the first in the long series of councils that mark the Church's history, and bears witness that the government of the Christian society was not to rest in the autocracy of a single will but in deliberative decision by those who represented the whole community. Strictly it was a provincial and not an oecumenical synod, called to decide what seemed a question of discipline rather than doctrine; but the ground of the argument gave it world-wide dogmatic importance, since if circumcision was necessary then faith in Christ was insufficient, which Paul saw and would not give way on for an hour.

How heated the debate was they read differently. Barnes objects to the English word: it is rather much inquiry or deliberation, since disputing imports heat and anger which the Greek need not carry, and there is no evidence of undue warmth. Robertson reads it the same way, that the Judaizers were given full opportunity to air their grievances, with no effort to shut off discussion. Calvin draws a lesson from the disagreement itself: though grave men and public teachers were chosen they could not agree at once, whereby appears how the Lord exercised his Church even then; some could not see the greatness of the matter, and being carried away with zeal for the law did not see into how deep a labyrinth they threw men's consciences. Wesley enters a qualification: it does not appear the debate was among the apostles themselves, but even if it had been, their final decision might still be from an unerring direction, since inspiration need not be instantaneous. Clarke names the party, the believing Pharisees, and reports that Cerinthus stood at their head, labouring to unite the law and the Gospel.

Whether Peter presided they answer with one voice. Henry says he did not pretend to any primacy in this synod, and was not master of the assembly nor so much as chairman. Ellicott says the same: his position is one of authority but not primacy, since he neither presides nor proposes a resolution, his authority being personal and moral and nothing more; nor can he believe, as the Romish theory implies, that Peter came from the imperial city to attend. Of a good while ago Lightfoot says Peter had an eye to the promise of the keys, that he might first open the door of the gospel to the Gentiles, the ancient days being the time when Jesus went in and out among them; Ellicott reckons ten or twelve years since Cornelius, with no record of where Peter had been meanwhile. Calvin divides the speech in two: the Gentiles must not be forced to keep the law, proved by the authority of God, and all man's salvation is overthrown if the conscience is once caught in that snare. Henry turns the occasion into a direction for pastors, to meet in solemn assembly for mutual advice when difficulties arise.
8:
The epithet for God at the head of the argument they mark as Peter's: Clarke says it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament except at the choosing of Matthias, Ellicott calls the recurrence characteristic of Peter, Robertson a late compound found only in those two places. What the witness consisted in Wesley puts in a line, that God bore them witness by giving them the Holy Ghost; Barnes, that he demonstrated he acknowledged them as his; Gill goes behind the gift to the heart, the searcher of hearts knowing with what sincerity Cornelius sent for Peter; Robertson adds that the Spirit was given before their baptism, and this was the Lord's doing.

Whether there was truly no difference Calvin will not leave unqualified. There was indeed some difference, he says, since the uncircumcised Gentiles were suddenly admitted to the covenant whereas the Jews had been prepared by circumcision unto faith; Peter's meaning is only that both were equally chosen. The others take it as it stands. Barnes says God showed the observance of these rites unnecessary to true conversion, and gave the Jews no advantage. Clarke calls the gift of the Spirit to the uncircumcised an evident proof that circumcision was no preparation for receiving the Gospel. Robertson puts it as a reversal: in faith and conversion God treated Jews as heathen and heathen as Jews. Ellicott finds in the words entire acceptance of what Paul had privately taught the three pillars of the Church, and notes that Romans reproduces almost the very words of Peter. Gill fills out the equality: no difference was put in the gifts or the special grace of the Spirit, the same faith, hope and love being given and the same inheritance. Wesley marks that the heart is purity's proper seat, and faith its means, apart from the Mosaic law.

What tempting God means they define four ways that accumulate. Ellicott makes it an experiment: to tempt God was to try whether his will, manifested in the acceptance of the Gentiles, or man's will, resisting it, was the stronger, and nothing but defeat could be the issue. Robertson makes it an insinuation and calls it a home-thrust: to require circumcision now implied that God had erred this time though right about Cornelius, and that they refused his guidance as Israel at Massah. Barnes makes it provocation, imposing rites on God's own people without his authority and against his manifest will. Gill makes it delay, hesitating and disputing where the case is plain. Calvin makes it weight: God is provoked as of set purpose when a heavier burden is laid on men than they can bear.

Which law the unbearable yoke means Clarke fixes carefully: not the moral law, of eternal obligation, but the ritual law, which through the multitude of its sacrifices was exceedingly burdensome, and but for a special providence over their fields and flocks could not have been borne at all; and he retails a rabbinic story in which Korah justifies his rebellion by parading the law's oppressiveness, the widow forbidden to plough with ox and ass together, to sow with divers seeds, and to reap her field's corners. Ellicott sets the words beside others: no words of Paul's about the Law could be stronger; they reproduce our Lord's language about the heavy burdens of Pharisaic tradition and his own easy yoke, and Paul echoed them in warning the Galatians against the yoke of bondage. Calvin follows Peter to the source: it were unmeet that the Gentiles, made equal with the holy people and vouchsafed adoption, should be rejected and God's liberality restrained, but Peter rises higher and pierces to the fountain, that those who tie men's salvation to works of law leave them no good hope and throw the world headlong into destruction. Wesley reduces it to a question: why provoke him by putting so heavy a yoke on their neck.
11:
Peter's last sentence they take as the hinge. Ellicott calls it the closing argument of a summary, since even the believing Pharisee was compelled to confess where his hope lay. Clarke reads it as an answer to the objection that God designed to save Jews by the law and Gentiles by the Gospel, and answers no. Wesley notices the words, that Peter does not say our Lord because in this solemn place he means the Lord of all, and that we Jews shall be saved even as they, not by the ceremonial law. Robertson calls the note thoroughly Pauline and renders it more exactly, that we believe we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus in like manner as they. Calvin sets the halves against each other as contraries, hope of salvation in the grace of Christ and subjection to the yoke of the law, a comparison which greatly sets out the justification Christ brings.

What the silence that followed meant they read as assent. Gill says there was a profound silence in the whole assembly, the brethren acquiescing by it. Robertson takes the aorist as ingressive, the multitude becoming silent because of Peter's speech, and the imperfect that follows as descriptive of rapt attention. Calvin says the Spirit of God so reigned in that assembly that they yielded forthwith to reason, the disputation having been hot before but ceasing once Peter had laid open God's counsel. Wesley notes that the miracles then reported confirmed Peter's word, and Clarke sets out the speech in numbered steps to show its facts could not be controverted. Barnes uses the silence to settle a question of composition: the multitude is evidently that of private Christians, not a synod of ministers and elders, since the church and the brethren are represented as present. Ellicott observes that the leaders had reserved their part to the last, the two apostles of the Gentiles being now called on to repeat publicly what they had narrated in private.

Which James this was they cannot settle. Barnes takes him for James the Less, the son of Alpheus; Ellicott for James the brother of the Lord; Calvin reports that some old writers make him the disciple surnamed Justus and Oblias, whose cruel death Josephus records, and wishes they had travailed to know the man rather than embellish him. Robertson adds that he was termed James the Just and reckoned a representative of the Hebraic against the Hellenistic wing, so that the Judaizers had counted on him as their champion.

That James and not Peter closed the debate they all press, and in one direction. Chrysostom says James was bishop, as they say, and therefore speaks last, fulfilling the rule of two or three witnesses, and notes the discretion with which he makes his argument good. Clarke says he was evidently president of the council and is generally called bishop of Jerusalem: the rest gave their opinion, but James alone pronounced the definitive sentence, which he would not have done had Peter been head of the apostles. Barnes puts it negatively: the whole transaction shows Peter had no such authority as is pretended for him, since otherwise his opinion would have been followed without debate, and James had an authority not less than his. Ellicott says James occupies a position clearly of pre-eminence, justifying the title of Bishop of Jerusalem later writers give him, since no one speaks after him. On the name Gill denies that Simeon means the aged man who took Christ in his arms, long since dead, and takes it of Simon Peter; Wesley adds that James, apostle of the Hebrews, calls Peter by his Hebrew name; Ellicott makes more of it, that the old Hebrew form instead of the familiar Simon was natural in a Galilean speaker and is presumptive evidence of a report from notes made at the time.
15:
That James answers Peter's fact with Scripture they all mark, and Calvin draws the lesson: the apostles took nothing to themselves imperiously but reverently followed the word of God, counting it no disgrace to profess themselves scholars of the Scripture. Clarke puts the division plainly: Peter asserted the fact, James shows it to be the fulfilment of what the prophets declared, and Wesley says the same in fewer words. Gill observes that several prophecies speak of the calling of the Gentiles but James produced one; Robertson says he cites Amos alone, and from the Greek; Ellicott notes the habit of quoting without naming the prophet, and that Stephen had already quoted him.

How far the citation departs from the Hebrew is the difficulty here, and they meet it three ways. Barnes is precise: the seventeenth verse is quoted literally from the Greek, but in the sixteenth only the general sense is kept, so the whole is literal from neither. Clarke offers a textual explanation: the verses stand nearly as in the best Greek editions, which differ considerably from the Hebrew, and where the Hebrew has that they may possess the remnant of Edom the translators evidently found a verb meaning to seek rather than to possess. Ellicott leaves the alternative open: they either paraphrased to give a wider meaning or read a different text. Calvin waves the detail aside on principle: because the place is not cited word for word we must see what difference there is, though it is not necessary to examine straitly the diversity of words, so long as the prophecy fitly agrees with the matter in hand. Lightfoot cuts across the question by an argument about language, holding that it will hardly be denied that James spoke here in Hebrew, that is, the Syriac tongue; and on the fallen tabernacle he brings a rabbinic exchange in which the Messiah is asked after as the son of the fallen.

Whose words the next sentence is Gill settles at once: known unto God are all his works are the words of James and not of Amos. Robertson agrees that James adds them, perhaps with a reminiscence of Isaiah, his point being that the purpose set forth in Amos is an old one. Calvin calls it an anticipation, put in to remove the hatred novelty might raise, the sudden change being liable to suspicion. Clarke says it means this is no new counsel of God, who had purposed from the calling of Israel to make the Gentiles partakers of the same grace. Wesley infers the same from the prophecy and its accomplishment: what God knew from eternity ought not to be thought new or strange. Ellicott notes that the better manuscripts give his work in the singular, the great work of the government and education of mankind, an implicit answer to the charge of innovation. Barnes puts it as method rather than polemic: God sees everything future, knows what he will accomplish, and has a plan.

How much authority James claims divides them squarely. Gill says he did not impose his sense but proposed it, and Barnes agrees that the words are a judge's usual language in delivering an opinion but do not imply that James assumed authority to settle the case. Clarke takes the opposite view: there is an authority here that does not appear in Peter's speech, and it was felt and bowed to by all the council, the decree James proposed being adopted. Robertson goes with him, calling it a summing up by the President of the Conference. Ellicott stands between, allowing the tone of one who speaks with authority while insisting that what follows is offered not as a decree but as a resolution submitted to the apostles and elders. Calvin raises a different difficulty: James seems contrary to himself in denying that the Gentiles ought to be troubled and then prescribing certain things.
20:
On what ground the four things were forbidden Lightfoot puts most sharply: were they forbidden under one notion, that the Gentiles might not offend the Jews, or was something else interwoven, that they might not relapse into heathenism? He divides them: the pollutions of idols and fornication to the second, things strangled and blood to the first. Calvin says the food rules were of themselves indifferent, yet had something in them beyond other rites of the law, since the Lord straitly commands us to eschew what contradicts the external profession of faith. Barnes makes it expediency: to partake might not be morally wrong, but it would give occasion for scandal, and so abstinence was advised. Ellicott calls the measure a compromise: the Gentiles could not complain that the burden was grievous, and the Pharisee section could not refuse admission on conditions by which they had already admitted the proselytes of the gate.

Why these four Ellicott answers from Jewish precedent: the rules found a place among the seven precepts traditionally ascribed to Noah, held binding on all mankind while the Law bound Israel only, and therefore thought sufficient for the proselytes of the gate. What pollutions of idols covers he then works out: any participation, publicly or privately, in idolatrous rites, so that one acting on the rule must refrain from entering a temple and dislodge the statues of the gods from his house and gardens, Zeus and Artemis and Hermes becoming abominations to him. Barnes and Clarke keep to the narrower sense of sacrificial meat, Barnes noting that such flesh was often sold in the markets, so that whether Christians might partake became an important question, and Clarke that not only idolatry was forbidden but the knowing eating of things offered in sacrifice and the joining with idolaters in their feasts.

Why fornication stands among ceremonial rules is the difficulty they feel most. Barnes says commentators have been greatly perplexed to find a violation of the moral law, about which there could be no dispute, among violations of the ceremonial. Wesley answers from heathen opinion: even the philosophers did not account it any fault, and it was particularly frequent in the worship of their idols, on which account the two are named together. Lightfoot answers from Christian practice, wondering at the heart and forehead of those who not only practised but taught diametrically contrary to this decree, and asking with what paint the Balaamites and Jezebelites could beautify it, whether by pretending the liberty of the gospel or abusing the love it commands.

What the closing verse about Moses is for Calvin says has been badly expounded. The others take the common reading: Ellicott says the conjunction gives the reason for writing to the Gentiles and not to the Jews, who heard the Law every Sabbath and needed no instruction; Clarke says the same; Wesley, that to the Jews we need write nothing on these heads since they hear the law continually; Barnes, that the law prohibiting these things was read constantly; and Gill traces the practice back to the times of Ezra. Robertson turns the fact the other way, making it the reason why the four things are named at all, since synagogues in every city meant that Gentile Christians would give constant offence by neglecting them. Calvin's own reading differs: James teaches that ceremonies cannot be abolished so quickly, as it were at the first dash, because the Jews had long been acquainted with the law and Moses had his preachers, so it behoved them to redeem concord for a short time until the liberty gotten by Christ might by little and little appear more plainly; it was meet, as the proverb has it, that the old ceremonies be buried with some honour. He adds that some gather from the place that circumcision ought still to be observed among the Jews, and that they reason unfitly.
22:
What part the whole church had they weigh carefully, and it matters most to Ellicott: the words show the position occupied by the laity, since if they concurred in the letter it must have been submitted to their approval, and the right to approve involves the power to reject. Wesley draws the same inference in a clause, that the whole church had a part in it, and that chosen men were sent to put beyond dispute that this was the judgment of the apostles and all the brethren. Clarke divides the labour: James determined what ought to be done, the whole assembly how it should be done. Barnes says all the Christians assembled concurred; Robertson supposes a unanimous vote with the Judaizers probably abstaining, and calls the proposal of James an irenicon that commended itself to the whole assembly; Gill says his advice was approved by the whole body and they agreed unanimously. Henry says much more was likely said than is recorded, but at length it was brought to a head and the advice James gave was universally approved. Calvin reads the same fact as a lesson in temper: the tempest was made calm not without the singular grace of God, so that after thorough discussion they all agreed in sound doctrine, and the modesty of the common people appears in their referring the matter to the judgment of others.

What the letter is Ellicott states most strongly: unless we assume deliberate fraud, what follows is clearly the transcript of a document, the first in the long list of decrees and canons and encyclical letters that mark the Church's history. Barnes is careful about the plural, that writing letters does not mean more than one epistle, and glosses the greeting as a word expressing their desire for the happiness of those addressed; Gill guards the phrase the other way, that the messengers were not amanuenses but had the letter put into their hands when written; Robertson says a committee of four carried it. Clarke notes for whom it was not written: there was no occasion to send such a letter to the brethren of the Jews, since the law read so long in their synagogues taught them these things, so the epistle goes exclusively to the Gentiles.

Whose proposal the decree follows Wesley makes into an argument: the whole conduct of the affair plainly shows that the Church in those days had no conception of Peter's primacy or of his being chief judge in controversies, since the decree is drawn up not according to his proposal but according to that of James. It is the conclusion the others drew from the order of the speeches, now taken from the drafting.

How the troublers are handled they all remark, in different registers. Calvin praises the impartiality: there was no respect of persons among these holy men, which always corrupts sound judgment, for they confess that there were knaves of their own company and yet do not flatter them through corrupt favour. Ellicott notices the courtesy, that the names are wisely and charitably suppressed. Robertson calls the sentence a direct blow at the Judaizers in delicate language, since it speaks as though the trouble had arisen only at Antioch and not also at Jerusalem in open meeting. Clarke presses the awkward fact that the men who produced these disputations at Antioch had gone out from the apostles at Jerusalem and were of that church, zealous for the law and yet, strange to tell, conscientious in that zeal. Barnes glosses the charge: they troubled them with doctrines, disturbing their minds and producing contentions, and the word rendered subverting occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Gill says the report came by Paul and Barnabas, sent to acquaint them with the state of the case. Wesley closes on style: the simplicity, weightiness and conciseness of this letter are highly observable.
25:
Why the letter praises its bearers Calvin explains as a countermeasure: the praises are set against the slanders by which the false apostles had essayed to bring Paul and Barnabas out of credit. The others weigh the commendation: Barnes calls it a noble testimony to their character, Clarke a high one, since they had already suffered much and exposed their lives to imminent danger; Wesley notes only that the words are spoken of Paul and Barnabas, and Robertson renders the participle literally, that they had handed over their lives. Ellicott draws an inference about the proceedings, that the narrative of the hairbreadth escapes at Pisidian Antioch and Lystra must have been laid before the Church. Gill supplies them, the persecution that expelled them from Pisidian Antioch and the stoning at Lystra where Paul was left for dead. Why two more men were sent Clarke explains as proof: Judas and Silas could witness by word of mouth and so show the letter was not forged, and Barnes says they would confirm all by their own statements.

What the claim to the Spirit's concurrence amounts to they take with one voice. Barnes calls it a strong and undoubted claim to inspiration, the Spirit having been promised with special reference to the church's organisation. Clarke says the council had met under the Spirit's direction, consulted under his influence, and gave forth their decree from his especial inspiration. Robertson calls it a definite claim that the church in this action had the Spirit's guidance, a fact plain to them from what had taken place. Ellicott derives it from the character of the measure, one of wisdom and charity, which the apostles could not ascribe to any other source than the Spirit who gives a right judgment in all things. Calvin guards the order of the names: in joining themselves with the Holy Ghost they attribute nothing to themselves apart, the speech importing that the Holy Ghost was captain, guide and governor. Gill grounds the confidence in the spirit of prayer among them and the power attending their deliberation.

Whether the necessary things were permanently binding is where they part. Wesley says plainly that all were necessary for that time, but that the first was not necessary long and the direction concerning it was therefore repealed by the same Spirit, as the former Epistle to the Corinthians shows. Clarke will have none of that latitude: they were necessary howsoever burdensome, and if the Gentiles did not keep from them they would do ill, that is, sin against God whose Spirit had commanded them. Wesley excepts one item and argues it at length, that the eating of blood was never permitted the children of God from the beginning of the world, since from Adam to Noah no man ate flesh at all and therefore none ate blood. Robertson sets the weight against what was gained: in comparison with the freedom won this burden is light.

Why the wording changes between resolution and letter Ellicott alone observes: the specific term for meats offered to idols replaces the more general word James had used, and the change, if the two are not simply equivalent, may favour the Gentiles by narrowing the prohibition. Gill and Barnes take the substitution as explanatory, the later phrase explaining what was meant by pollutions of idols. On the delivery Calvin returns to who may judge: to admit the whole multitude to the reading was the most lawful dealing, for if controversy falls out in the doctrine of faith it is meet that judgment be referred to the learned and the godly. Ellicott thinks it natural to infer that they returned as they had come, through Samaria and Phoenicia, gladdening the disciples on the way; Robertson supposes religious services at their dismissal and perhaps an escort; Gill notes that the four were dismissed by the apostles, elders and church at Jerusalem.
31:
How so short a letter could console Calvin raises against himself: seeing it is so short and contains nothing but a bare narration, what consolation could they have by it? His answer is that there was no small matter of consolation in it, once they knew what had been determined. Clarke says it was no small thing to have a question of such weight decided by an apostolic council over which the Spirit presided. Barnes says they acquiesced and rejoiced that they were not to be subjected to the burdensome rites of the Jewish religion. Ellicott finds the consolation in the reader as much as the letter, since it was probably read out by one who was himself the son of consolation; Robertson notes the reading was public, and Gill that the brethren read it, not the men who carried it.

What the two men were they explain by their title. Barnes says being prophets implies they had been preachers before they came, though what the office precisely was is not easy to ascertain. Clarke reduces it to teachers, and Gill guards the other way, that prophets are not only such as foretell. Robertson calls them forth-speakers for Christ, and Ellicott notices the wordplay, that the verb rendered exhorted is the one from which the Greek for consolation was formed. Calvin explains why they were sent at all: to testify by word what the letters contained and more, since otherwise so short a letter would not have been sent on so weighty a matter.

Whether Silas stayed behind by Scripture or by a copyist's gloss divides them four to one. Barnes says the verse is wanting in many manuscripts and in the Syriac, Arabic and Coptic versions, and is regarded as spurious by Mill, Griesbach and others. Clarke adds the Slavonic, the Vulgate and some of the fathers. Robertson says it is absent from the chief uncials and the Vulgate and is clearly an addition. Ellicott gives the motive: the better manuscripts omit the verse, which a later copyist probably supplied to explain how Silas came to be at hand a few verses on. Gill alone treats the sentence as text: Silas had leave to go and was dismissed with Judas, and doubtless intended to go, but for some reason stayed. Clarke says as much even while rejecting the verse, that both had liberty to depart but Silas chose to remain. How long they stayed nobody knows, though Gill reports that the Arabic version makes it a year.

Where the quarrel with Peter falls they place here, though the chapter does not record it. Barnes says it is probable that the unhappy incident recorded in Galatians occurred here; Robertson says the same and adds that Paul takes the initiative in what follows as leader, all the more so if the rebuke had already taken place; Wesley states it flatly, that Peter came down from Jerusalem and Paul withstood him to the face for separating himself from the Gentiles. Ellicott reckons the received chronology to make the interval somewhat more than a year, and among the many others at Antioch would count the prophets named earlier and not improbably the martyr Ignatius. Chrysostom draws a lesson from the same crowd, bidding us observe again their humility, in that they let others also take part in the preaching. Calvin turns to the proposal and marks what it shows of Paul: he laboured at Antioch profitably, but remembering that he was an apostle ordained of God and not the pastor of one particular place, he kept the course of his calling. Henry sets the two halves of the chapter against each other: one unhappy difference among the brethren, of a public nature, brought to a good issue, and now a private quarrel between two ministers, no less men than Paul and Barnabas, not compromised indeed, yet ending well.
37:
Why Barnabas wanted Mark they trace to kinship, and most think it a weakness. Clarke says Mark was his sister's son and that natural affection might have led to the partiality mentioned; Barnes says the same; Wesley reduces it to a word, kinsman. Ellicott is gentler: the ties of relationship led him to wish another trial of his kinsman, and he saw extenuating circumstances which Paul could not recognise. Gill adds what might be urged for Mark, that his mother had received the saints into her house in a time of danger. On the verb they differ: Gill reports copies reading he would or was willing rather than determined, Ellicott says the Greek is hardly so strong and prefers was minded, and Robertson insists on the imperfect against the received aorist, so Barnabas willed and wished and stuck to it.

Why Paul refused they explain alike. Barnes says he could not confide in Mark's perseverance amid the toils and perils of the journey, and that why Mark had departed is not known, though evidently for some cause Paul did not think satisfactory. Wesley puts it as trust: it was not right to trust again one who had deserted them and shrunk from the labour of converting the very people they were going to confirm. Gill says the word implies Paul did not think him a fit person.

What the sharpness was, and whose, they dispute. Barnes says the word is that from which our paroxysm is derived, may denote any excitement of mind, and is used in a good sense in Hebrews, but here means a violent altercation. Clarke shows how little the Greek says: for the whole clause there stands only that there was therefore a paroxysm, from a verb meaning to whet. Robertson keeps the metaphor of the blade and applies it without mercy: this son of consolation loses his temper in a dispute over his cousin. Wesley enters the one clear dissent: nothing in the text implies the sharpness was on both sides, and it is far more probable it was not, since Paul, who had the right, maintained it with love. Ellicott explains the heat by the affection behind it, a friendship begun in boyhood and cemented by a great work they shared. Calvin will not soften it: a doleful disagreement which ought to make all the godly afraid, since their society had been consecrated by a heavenly oracle and they had long laboured of one mind under the yoke to which the Lord had tied them.

Whether the narrative takes Paul's side turns on a single clause. Clarke reports that much stress has been laid on the brethren recommending Paul and Silas to the grace of God and not Barnabas, and doubts the words will bear it; Wesley presses it the other way, that we do not find Barnabas stayed for this. Ellicott draws a consequence from the choice of Silas: even if the verse about his remaining be an interpolation, it is clear he had stayed when the other delegates went back, itself a proof of his interest in the mission work. Robertson says Paul chose him as successor to Barnabas, not to Mark, who had no place in his plans. On the last verse Barnes says confirming means strengthening by instruction and exhortation, with no reference to the rite, while Ellicott, allowing the general sense, holds that since the bestowal of spiritual gifts by laying on of hands was a chief part of the work, the word approaches the later technical idea. Ellicott adds that Cilicia had not been visited on the first journey, so its churches must have been founded during Paul's residence at Tarsus; Clarke says the object was to establish young converts, whose faith the council's decision strengthened; Robertson observes that Paul took the opposite course from the first tour, going forth with heart-aches and high hopes mingled together.
